name: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasm

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: FIGO Diagnostic Criteria for Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia

criteria.description: Elevated or plateauing serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels for more than 6 weeks after evacuation of molar pregnancy
Histological confirmation of invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, or placental site trophoblastic tumor
Radiological evidence of metastatic lesions in lungs, brain, liver, or other organs
Abnormal uterine bleeding or enlarged uterus inconsistent with gestational age

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Persistent elevated or plateauing hCG levels plus either histopathological confirmation or radiological evidence of metastasis
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis often relies on a combination of clinical, biochemical, histological, and imaging findings.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Persistent elevated serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
Enlarged uterus disproportionate to gestational age
searchTerms: uterus bigger than expected for pregnancy
anemia caused by heavy uterine bleeding
blood loss anemia due to uterine bleeding

common.symptomName: Shortness of breath due to pulmonary metastases
searchTerms: shortness of breath from lung tumors
coughing up blood from lung tumors
blood in sputum due to lung metastases

occasional.symptomName: Headache or neurological deficits from brain metastases
searchTerms: headache and neurological problems from brain tumors
right upper belly pain from liver metastases

occasional.symptomName: Hyperthyroidism symptoms due to hCG cross-reactivity
searchTerms: hyperthyroidism signs due to hormone cross-reactivity
visual disturbances due to choroidal metastases
epileptic episodes due to brain lesions
severe pregnancy high blood pressure syndrome

imaging: Ultrasound showing heterogeneous uterine mass with cystic spaces
Chest X-ray or CT showing pulmonary nodules
MRI or CT brain for cerebral metastases
genetic: No specific germline mutations identified; disease arises from abnormal trophoblastic proliferation
other: Histopathology showing trophoblastic proliferation and invasion

distinguishingFeatures: Absence of intrauterine mass with ultrasound
Acute abdominal pain and hemodynamic instability
Well-circumscribed solid uterine mass on imaging
Lack of rapid growth or metastasis

redFlags: Rapidly rising or plateauing serum hCG after pregnancy
Evidence of metastatic disease on imaging
Severe abnormal uterine bleeding causing hemodynamic instability
references: Seckl MJ, Sebire NJ, Berkowitz RS. Gestational trophoblastic disease: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up. Ann Oncol. 2013 Jul;24 Suppl 6:vi39-50.
Goldstein DP, Berkowitz RS. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia: 2021 update. Gynecol Oncol. 2021 Mar;160(3):661-668.
